answer.recommendation: For a healthy 30-year-old lifter, creatine monohydrate at standard doses is well supported as safe and has not been shown to impair kidney function; a pooled analysis covered 3 to 25 g/day for up to 5 years without a change in glomerular filtration rate [1]. A 12-month trial of 5 g/day found no difference in creatinine clearance versus placebo [2].
answer.why: A high-grade meta-analysis of 21 randomized placebo-controlled trials (n=1212 healthy adults) found no change in glomerular filtration rate (mean difference 0.9 mL/min, 95% CI -1.8 to 3.6) [1]. Adverse events were similar, 8.1% with creatine versus 7.9% with placebo [3]. A moderate-grade 12-month RCT in 100 healthy strength-training adults found no difference in creatinine clearance, liver enzymes or blood lipids versus placebo [4]. Serum creatinine rose slightly, which is expected from creatine metabolism rather than a sign of kidney damage [5]. The opposing evidence is a rat study at a high dose, which showed more renal inflammation, and it is very low grade and not in healthy adults [6]. A single case report of interstitial nephritis involved 20 g/day plus several other supplements, and a causal role for creatine could not be established [7].

positions.stance: Long-term creatine supplementation is safe for healthy adults and does not impair kidney function
positions.best_counterargument: A rat study found more renal inflammation with high-dose creatine (inflammatory cell infiltration score 2.1 vs 0.6), and a case report described acute interstitial nephritis after 20 g/day creatine with other supplements. Both are very-low-grade evidence, though, and the case report could not establish that creatine caused the injury.

answer.what_would_change_this: Large human trials showing kidney harm in healthy adults at standard doses would change this. Having existing kidney disease would also change it, since the findings do not cover that group [8].
answer.applies_to_you: You are a healthy 30-year-old training for strength, which closely matches the 12-month trial population of healthy strength-training adults [9]. The trials did not report subgroups with dehydration or high protein intake, and the meta-analysis did not state age or sex [8]. The conclusion applies to healthy adults only, so check with a clinician first if you have kidney disease.
answer.practical_protocol: Use creatine monohydrate at 5 g/day, the dose used in the 12-month trial that showed no change in creatinine clearance [2]. Avoid stacking it with many other supplements, since the one case report involved 20 g/day plus several other supplements [7]. If you have kidney blood tests, tell the clinician you take creatine, because serum creatinine can rise slightly [5].
answer.disclaimer: This is general, evidence-based training and nutrition information, not medical advice. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before making changes if you have a health condition, injury, or take medication.

output.rationale: A high-grade meta-analysis of 21 randomized placebo-controlled trials (n=1212 healthy adults, 3-25 g/day for up to 5 years) found no change in glomerular filtration rate (mean difference 0.9 mL/min, 95% CI -1.8 to 3.6) and similar adverse event rates (8.1% vs 7.9%). Both are very-low-grade and cannot show that creatine caused harm in humans. The harm side is right that serum creatinine rises slightly with creatine, which is expected from its metabolism, and that high-dose use alongside other supplements is less well characterized. The findings also report no subgroup data on dehydration or high protein intake, and they do not cover people with existing kidney disease, so the conclusion applies to healthy adults only.
